summary: Defines COSE header parameters that either carry X.509 certificates or refer to them, so COSE messages can identify keys through certificates. This extends the existing ways COSE can identify and transport keys.

eli5.summary: A message can come with a name badge from a trusted office, or just a note saying where to find the badge.

how to include certificate in cose message
subtitle: Four header parameters that let a COSE message carry an X.509 certificate or point to one.

tldr.problem: COSE had no consistent way to carry or refer to X.509 certificates, even though constrained devices are increasingly deployed inside existing X.509 PKIs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines header parameters x5bag, x5chain, x5t and x5u, plus sender variants for static-static ECDH, to carry certificates, hash them, or give a URI for them.
tldr.outcome: COSE applications can reuse existing certificate trust infrastructure, as long as they treat the certificates as untrusted input and integrity protect the end-entity certificate.

today: RFC 9360 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 9052.

sections.title: Why COSE Needs Certificate Headers
sections.content:
When the COSE specifications RFC 8152 and RFC 9052 were written, the working group saw no use case that needed X.509 certificates. Since then, several cases have appeared, so applications need a documented and consistent way to handle them.

The RFC gives examples. A constrained device may carry a factory-installed certificate when it is enrolled in an existing X.509 PKI. EDHOC was written so that long-term certificates could authenticate devices. A secure messaging application built on COSE could use certificates to rely on well-established key management disciplines.
sections.eli5: Some small gadgets need to show an ID badge to prove who they are. This RFC says how to attach the badge to a message in a way everybody understands.

sections.title: The Four Header Parameters
sections.content:
Section 2 defines four header parameters. x5bag holds an unordered bag of certificates, which may include self-signed or even unrelated ones. x5chain holds an ordered array that starts with the end-entity certificate, followed by the certificate that signed it, and so on. The chain need not be complete if the relying party already has, or can find, the missing certificates.

x5t identifies the end-entity certificate by a hash (a thumbprint) and x5u gives a URI where the certificate can be fetched. Applications that use x5t MUST support SHA-256 for interoperability. The URI in x5u can point to a resource of type application/pkix-cert, application/pkcs7-mime with smime-type="certs-only", or application/cose-x509.

In COSE_Signature and COSE_Sign1 objects the parameters identify the certificate used to validate the signature. In COSE_recipient objects they identify the recipient's certificate.
sections.eli5: You can put the whole badge in the envelope, a stack of badges, just the badge's fingerprint, or a web address where the badge is kept.

sections.title: Encoding and Labels
sections.content:
A single certificate in x5bag or x5chain is a CBOR byte string holding the DER-encoded certificate. Several certificates are sent as a CBOR array of byte strings, one per certificate. The RFC gives the CDDL: COSE_X509 = bstr / [ 2*certs: bstr ] and COSE_CertHash = [ hashAlg: (int / tstr), hashValue: bstr ].

For x5t the first element names the hash algorithm using a value from the "COSE Algorithms" registry, and the second is the hash computed over the DER-encoded certificate. For x5u, the application/cose-x509 media type carries a CBOR sequence of COSE_X509 structures. Setting its usage parameter to chain marks the sequence as a certificate chain.
sections.eli5: Each badge is packed in its own little box, and the box labels follow a fixed format so any reader can open them.

sections.title: Sender Certificates for Static-Static ECDH
sections.content:
For static-static Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key agreement, the recipient's certificate is identified with the parameters above. The sender's certificate needs its own parameters, defined analogously: x5chain-sender, x5t-sender and x5u-sender. There is no sender version of the bag, because the same x5bag parameter would serve both sides.

These apply to the algorithms ECDH-SS+HKDF-256, ECDH-SS+HKDF-512, ECDH-SS+A128KW, ECDH-SS+A192KW and ECDH-SS+A256KW. Their structures and processing match x5chain, x5t and x5u.
sections.eli5: When two people each hold a badge, the sender needs separate slots for their own badge, so the two do not get mixed up.

sections.title: Trust and Security Rules
sections.content:
Certificates in x5bag and x5chain MUST be processed as untrusted input, and a self-signed certificate MUST NOT change the set of trust anchors without out-of-band confirmation. The relying party still validates the certificate, for example under the PKIX rules in RFC 5280. If trust cannot be established, the public key cannot be used.

The end-entity certificate MUST be integrity protected by COSE. That can be done by putting the parameter in the protected header, by pairing an unprotected x5bag, x5chain or x5u with a protected x5t, or by including the certificate in the external_aad. Without this, an attacker could mount an identity-misbinding attack by swapping in a certificate with someone else's public key.

Certificates reveal identities, and x5t and x5u are also permanent identifiers. COSE provides no identity protection by itself, so send it inside another protocol providing confidentiality if that matters.

Keys MUST be checked against the algorithm before use, and both signature validation and certificate validation MUST succeed before acting on a request. A retrieved x5u certificate that does not chain to an existing trust anchor MUST NOT be trusted unless specific conditions are met, and TLS, DTLS or OSCORE SHOULD be used for HTTP or CoAP retrieval.
sections.eli5: A badge is only a claim. You still check it with a trusted office, and you keep it sealed in the envelope so nobody swaps it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the four parameters in the "COSE Header Parameters" registry and the three sender parameters in the "COSE Header Algorithm Parameters" registry. It also registered the media type application/cose-x509, with an optional usage parameter that can be absent or set to chain.
sections.eli5: The numbers and names were written into the official list so nobody else uses them for something different.
